description: The image displays three pie charts labeled “easy,” “medium,” and “hard,” each illustrating the distribution of four categories—N+K+, N−K+, N−K−, and N+K−—across different difficulty levels of a task, likely related to geometric knowledge reasoning with large language models as suggested by the paper title. The legend on the right identifies N+K+ as teal, N−K+ as beige, N−K− as orange, and N+K− as red. In the “easy” chart, N−K+ (beige) dominates at 45.9%, followed by N+K+ (teal) at 40.6%, N−K− (orange) at 10.1%, and N+K− (red) at 3.3%. The “medium” chart shows a more balanced distribution: N+K+ (teal) at 44.6%, N−K+ (beige) at 44.3%, N−K− (orange) at 7.2%, and N+K− (red) at 3.9%. In the “hard” chart, N−K− (orange) and N−K+ (beige) are nearly equal at 36.8% and 36.2% respectively, with N+K+ (teal) at 20.1% and N+K− (red) at 7.0%. All charts include percentage labels within each slice, and the “CoT” label beneath the charts may indicate that these results pertain to reasoning with Chain-of-Thought prompting. The visual structure suggests a shift in performance or strategy across difficulty levels, with easier tasks favoring N−K+ and harder tasks showing increased reliance on N−K− and N−K+.
